MN202611_1qm1qzzungt.t:
Jim Lembesis has been working on elevators in Chicago for 47 years

Some of them are angry. Nerves are frayed. Many of them are just relieved that he's here.

When a lift stops working in Chicago, frazzled building managers might get a visit from Jim Lembesis. For more than 47 years, Lembesis has repaired and upgraded lifts. He says he understands why staff and residents are so anxious to have things working again.

"They wait and they wait," says Lembesis, a field technician for Parkway Elevators. "There's a lot of frustration. Sometimes it's a repeat issue. It's a never-ending cycle, you know what I mean?"

The widely reported shortage of lift and escalator mechanics in the US, which is also a problem in many other countries, has got worse over time, he adds: "It's been like night and day compared to when I started."

Lift and escalator technicians "amaze" with their ability to fix things

Everyone needs a lift now and again. Some people depend on them – elderly residents of high-rise buildings, say, or wheelchair users.

Storm-damaged lifts in Hawaiian apartment blocks this year left some residents trapped , external in their homes for weeks. A lack of mechanics, and problems sourcing parts, were blamed for the repair delays.

In the US, the average salary for a lift mechanic , external is $110,000 (£83,000). And yet people in the industry say it is difficult to attract new workers.

Sure, says Lembesis, you do encounter some dangers in a job like this. There are risks of falling from a great height – or being electrocuted. Once, he was even hit on the head with an umbrella by an elderly lady after he rescued her from a stuck lift.

But there are so many skills to learn, and great camaraderie and knowledge-sharing among mechanics, he says. As one recruiter puts it, these technicians amaze people with their ability to fix things. They are like "wizards". The overall-clad shamans who know how to get modern life running again.

Nine times out of 10, the problem is with the doors, says Lembesis. These components repeatedly move back and forth. "People hit them with carts, and dirt and debris [falls into them]," says Lembesis. "[The doors] take the most beating."

Mechanics often keep various spare door parts in their vehicles, ready to use.

But technicians like Lembesis don't just have to get lifts working, they also have to verify the lifts are safe. He remembers one case, decades ago, getting called out to a burning building. His role was to ensure the lifts, which were being drenched with huge volumes of water, were still safe to use while firefighters tackled the blaze.

"I was there for 15 hours that night," he says. "Everyone, on the way out of the door, shook my hand."

In the US there's a four-year apprenticeship to become a lift technician

Finding good lift technicians is "becoming more difficult" says Matt Hollinshead, president of the US National Association for Elevator Contractors. "We have a four-year apprenticeship," he says. That's the first hurdle. And many states require certification or licensing before you can work on lifts.

"We have a vast array of equipment that has to be maintained in the United States." Some lifts are 100-years-old. As time goes on, the technological knowledge required to repair them only grows.

Hollinshead says that weeks or months-long delays to lift repairs are not typically due to staff shortages but that, in such cases, it's likely that a particular part isn't readily available. Manufacturing a replacement hydraulic cylinder takes six to 12 weeks, he notes.

But the lack of technicians does mean that that building managers might have to wait days before someone can even diagnose what's wrong with a lift after it stops working.

Hollinshead says teaching the basics of the trade in high schools or technical schools could entice more people into the role.

Matt Allred, a recruiter and host of The Elevator Careers Podcast, emphasises the many skills that lift mechanics require. "You're a little bit of a wizard, right? You show up and if you can fix it – 'Wow!'."

He blames major lift companies, in part, for locking down maintenance contracts, making it difficult or impossible for third-party repairers to intervene when a lift fails.

Two large lift manufacturers approached by BBC News declined interviews. The chief executive of Otis, one of the firms, said in May that her company was struggling to hire enough staff , external to meet demand. The firm also states on its website , external that the shortage of lift mechanics affects "almost every part of the world".

However, a spokesman for Otis claimed its "US talent pipeline" was healthy, and declined an interview.

Otis says it is happy with its supply of mechanics and engineers

Everyone else who spoke to BBC News said hiring was challenging in the US. Allred was recently contacted by a major lift company and asked to help them find a technician. "I was surprised that a major company would reach out to a little recruiting shop," he says, suggesting that this reflects the extent of the labour shortage.

That shortage is also a problem in the UK. "It is bad and getting worse," says Dave Cooper, president of the Chartered Institution of Building Services Engineers, who is also chief executive of a lift and escalator engineering consultancy.

"We've known food delivery companies to refuse to deliver to flats above the ground floor because the lift is out of service."

Offering better tax breaks to companies that train lift mechanics could help ensure that plenty of workers continue to enter the industry, he adds.

Training to be a lift mechanic is "not a quick route to competency – and it requires people to stick at it for the long term" says Karen Slade, head of assessment at the Lift and Escalator Industry Association (Leia).

Continued investment in training and attracting new workers is "essential", according to Leia. There are currently 259 active lift and escalator apprentices in the UK, the body adds.

Back in Chicago, Lembesis is working with two younger mechanics who have been "really good", he says, so there's at least some hope for the future.

He stresses again how rewarding he finds his work. The people for whom he fixes lifts tend to be very appreciative.

"I love that. You get that reaction from the customers," he says. "Without them, you got nothing."

MN202611_1fzb55j41md.t:
The wild landscape of Glencoe in Scotland is where Mohannad has found calm

After years toiling all day at a desk as an aerospace engineer in Istanbul, 26-year-old Mohannad Najjar decided to swap his screen for a degree in nature and theology in Cambridge and a volunteering gig as a scout leader.

He walks in the countryside every weekend and has hiked in wild locations in the Scottish Highlands, which he credits with helping him think clearly.

"I just want to see something that's untouched, to be in nature," he says. "When you come in from a hike or a walk, you just feel different."

Najjar is one of a growing number of young hikers in the UK. Nearly 9% of 16-34 year-olds are regular hill walkers or hikers, according to Sport England, up from 2.3% eight years ago.

Watch: Why we're swapping screens for scenery

Many young walkers' groups from Inverness to Nottinghamshire have seen their membership rise over the past two years, according to the Ramblers walking charity.

Demand has nearly doubled for a course it offers teaching map and compass skills to 18-25 year-olds.

Many who sign up want to ditch their phones and no longer rely on a blue dot to navigate, says Alistair Cooper, who leads the Out There Award programme.

"There's a cohort that missed out on outdoorsy, fun stuff during Covid. They want to get out and explore - but often don't know where to start."

Some 83% of people in the UK live in towns and cities, according to the UN, where research suggests noise, traffic, stress and information overload put huge demands on our brains, affecting our mental health.

"Nature is the environment we are adapted to, and being close to it brings benefits such as improved wellbeing, brain function and physical performance," says Dr Danny Longman, lecturer in human evolutionary physiology from Loughborough University.

"There is a theory that simply paying attention to trees and leaves allows our brains to recover," he says.

For Deborah Odutayo, her navigation skills are now one of her biggest achievements

Environmental science student Deborah Odutayo, 24, described going through "an identity crisis".

"I didn't see myself as someone who works behind a desk from 9 to 5," she said.

After solo travelling, Odutayo had dreams of living abroad but didn't know how to finance them. So she decided to change her mindset.

"I just need to be outside, essentially. That's how I started like doing solo hikes and stuff. It feels very therapeutic - mostly for my mental health."

She's since hiked in Kent and the Peak District, among other locations, and camped with an outdoor group in Dorset.

Learning how to get around without using her phone or digital maps is something she is proud of, saying it feels "more intentional and grounding".

No matter the weather, Miranda Chambers-Reid gets outside any time she can

Walking gives people "an instant friend group" when life is in flux, says Miranda Chambers-Reid, who leads a Ramblers' walking group for people in their 20s and 30s in Sheffield.

"They don't want all of their friends to be work friends or old uni friends," she says.

As a mum of a seven-year-old, she made a similar decision when she joined: "I thought, I don't want all of my friends to be mum friends."

Over the last two years, the group has increased from 250 members to 350.

For some it's more about a sense of achievement says Chambers-Reid, who herself covers about 30 miles of walking a week.

"I work in an office and I can't see the sky so whenever possible I will be outside."

For Sej Chauhan, 27, her walking group is about making connections while keeping costs down.

"There's a growing interest in socialising in ways that don't involve drinking alcohol or spending lots of money," she says.

Chauhan set up Girls Who Walk in her home town of Leicester after a lonely year spent studying in Bristol.

To make that experience easier for others, the group's focus is on walking in parks, talking and female companionship. And there's always a stop for coffee.

In two years, the group has grown to more than 300 members - most are 25-35 years old.

"There's no pressure, no barriers with walking," Chauhan says. "Social media can often fill the void outside of work and home, but it doesn't provide the connection that people are craving."

Walking together in Leicester's Victoria Park - the Girls Who Walk group

Not everyone can access green space easily or has the time to go hiking because of work or childcare commitments.

Here are Longman's tips for getting your nature fix as close as possible to home:

Move in nature - an urban park or garden will do

Listen to the sounds of the elements, like wind, rain, birdsong

Smell the distinctive scent of pine forests, breathe in the outdoors

If you are indoors, bring the sounds and imagery of nature into your home using apps

MN202611_14dcvq94t4v.t:
Camilo Duran's 15-goal haul this season has made him an invaluable player for a Celtic side fighting for European progression

"Duran is priceless for us at the moment".

It would be difficult for a football manager to muster up a higher compliment for one of his players - given he should know exactly how much he did cost - but Celtic boss Martin O'Neill was rightly effusive in his praise for Camilo Duran.

With 15 goals in 23 appearances, six assists, and another late European winner on Thursday, the Colombian was once again the main man for a struggling Celtic side.

His double against Besiktas breathed life into their Europa League campaign last time out, and his late leap to nod in the winner against Torreense kept it alive.

Duran, 24, started on the bench but was brought on with just over half an hour to go as O'Neill watched his side labour against a team currently 13th in the Portuguese second tier.

Celtic would still be searching for their first European win were it not for their summer arrival from Qarabag, whose goals have played a key part in keeping his team within touching distance of a play-off spot with three fixtures to play.

"He's taken on this mantle of being the man and he's been fantastic," said O'Neill, who started Duran on the bench. "We tried a similar approach against Besiktas.

"Sometimes by the time Duran gets subbed on, you could be behind. But I think that's the sign of a brilliant player, he'll do something.

"He's not a big guy but he's just a super footballer, a super, super footballer."

'He's priceless for us' - O'Neill on match winner Duran

Duran's summer arrival was overshadowed when, just over a fortnight later, a club-record fee was paid to Bodo Glimt for another striker, Kasper Hogh.

While recent weeks have been dominated by debates over Duran or Hogh , the debate now seems settled, with the Colombian operating on a different level from his striking counterpart.

Anyone watching Celtic in Portugal would have watched Hogh find space a handful of times in the area, but repeatedly fail to find a team-mate or trouble the goalkeeper. Duran didn't need to be asked twice.

"I don't know how many touches he got, but he had the telling touch," James McFadden said on Sportsound post-match.

Duran's goals have also proved decisive in securing domestic points against Falkirk and Hibernian, and with Celtic just a point clear of Rangers, he is indeed invaluable.

Despite his late header giving the thousands of travelling Celtic fans a thrilling end to a relatively turgid game, the intervention is another significant moment in a season that is threatening to unravel if individual performances fail to continue papering over glaring deficiencies across the park.

If the lively Jota - who lasted 74 minutes - was not creating chances, tormenting full-backs or digging out enticing crosses in the first half, Celtic seemed without any real plan of attack.

Yang and Luke McCowan's involvements were limited at best, Hogh's chance to stake a claim was sub-par to be kind, and there was no driving force from the middle of the park to show some impetus.

Arithmetically, Celtic can still finish in any position in the Europa League table. But if they are to claim a playoff or automatic qualification spot, they will need Duran to remain in such a rich vein of form.

Duran spares Celtic's blushes against Portuguese second-tier side Torreense

Celtic news, views and analysis all in one place

Brian: Embarrassed by that performance, I know that there no easy games in Europe, couldn't pass the ball, not fit enough, no style of play and poorly coached. The club is in decline.

John: Celtic are just an average side these days - there should be no expectation.

Ted: That was just embarrassing. The 31st team in Portugal made us look ordinary. Go now Martin with dignity intact and preserve your achievements. Thus mob will drag you down.

Allan: Outclassed and out paced by Torreense, Celtic played poorly with a lot of comedy of errors in their play. But Yippee hee, Celtic. Won with a late goal from Duran.

Liam: This can't go on any further now, regardless of the result. MON is done and the coaching staff are done. Booing substitutions is the end, never mind a performance like this against second division opposition. The board can resign too.

Alec: Total embarrassment. Barring Jota, there was a complete lack of creativity, quality, urgency and belief. Time for the board to make the right decisions, get a new manager in and get rid of at least 10 of those players on show tonight.

MN202611_1xklkxeehe8.t:
Self-confessed foodie Catherine says the sense of freedom she gets from picking where and when she eats is "empowering"

Catherine Smith is perusing the menu at a high-end Mediterranean restaurant she has been excited to try. She has a new outfit on, and as she sips her rosé, she looks across at the empty seat - bliss.

"I think what is so special about solo dining is that you don't have to wait for people to make those plans. You can go out and do them yourself," says the 23-year-old.

The self-confessed foodie is part of a growing trend of people booking tables for one - not because they're away with work but as a treat.

As food trends analyst Charles Banks puts it: "[Eating alone] is becoming an intentional act, a little pocket of independence, indulgence and self-care."

We spoke to solo dining fans and hospitality industry experts about how the trend is shaping the restaurant experience and asked if you would book a table for one.

Solo dining: Would you book a table for one?

Catherine, from Yorkshire, began dining solo at university and now does it at least once a month, choosing high-end restaurants she would not usually go to with friends and family.

She has been to a range of places both in the UK and abroad, doing "lots of research" to find new spots, typically spending £100 to £200 per meal.

"I think because a lot of my friends are vegan or vegetarian, I find that difficult sometimes because I'm quite a big meat eater," she says.

"I find it nice to be able to go out and pick a restaurant where I haven't had to scour through the menu to make sure that it's suitable for them."

Catherine says the sense of freedom she gets from picking where and when she eats "feels empowering".

"It definitely feels like not only a form of self-care but also a form of female liberation."

While solo dining Catherine likes to read, journal or simply enjoy the peace and quiet

Online booking platform OpenTable says it covers more than 5,000 restaurants in the UK. It says solo dining makes up the smallest proportion of its bookings in the UK but it is the fastest-growing category.

Figures from 1 January to 31 August this year saw a rise of 23% in solo bookings compared to the same time period a year ago. It did not provide the data to the BBC to verify.

Nishi Singh was an avid solo diner when she lived in London, but found it wasn't widely accepted after moving to Delhi.

"Someone approached me and said that they assumed I'd been stood up," she tells BBC World Service's The Food Chain podcast.

"It sparked a conversation about the culture around solo dining in Delhi and I was really shocked to hear that it's not really something people do."

A couple of days later, she started documenting her solo dining experience on social media.

"Quite a lot of people have reached out and said that this is something they'd like to do and they're too scared to do it themselves," she says.

Ruth Alexander hears from solo diners - some who find peace and joy in a table for one, and others who would much rather not be alone

Banks, joint managing director of The Food People, a food trends and ideas agency, says that while solo dining isn't a "new consumer behaviour", changes in society mean it has become "almost aspirational".

But he notes that not every restaurant has welcomed the trend.

"A single diner could therefore feel like an inefficient use of a table rather than a customer the restaurant actively wanted."

SoloTable, a website that helps identify restaurants suitable for solo diners, found that one in eight of 178 restaurants it surveyed in London did not accept online reservations from solo diners.

Catherine says she has previously been turned away. "There are a lot of restaurants that I've wanted to go to before where they don't actually allow solo diners. And I've always found that to be really disappointing."

Yousaf thinks solo diners could produce another useful business stream for restaurants

However, some restaurants like Jungli, an Indian restaurant in Newcastle upon Tyne, is working to attract solo diners.

Co-founder and director Yousaf Khalid has included high tables and bar seats in his recently opened restaurant. They also have charging points for laptops and phones.

"We want people to feel comfortable in these sorts of environments, being able to walk in on their own," he says.

He has hired staff with "bigger personalities" to engage customers in conversation but they also know when to leave diners alone if they want a more solitary experience.

Catherine urges anyone who fancies solo dining to give it a go.

"Food is a great way to bring people together, but it's also a great way to have good experiences on your own.

"I think with time, people will see and will start to accept it as something that's more normal."

Additional reporting by Jemma Crew and Emma Jackson.

MN202611_3324tqz39o.t:
Watch: Man wrongly sentenced to death says Met Police ruined his life

A Kenyan woodcutter who was wrongly sentenced to death over an attack on a British couple has told the BBC that actions by London's Metropolitan Police involved in the case destroyed his life.

Somali gunmen broke into David and Judith Tebbutt's beach bungalow on the Kenyan coast in 2011. They shot David dead and abducted Judith, holding her captive in Somalia for six months.

Met detectives flew to Kenya to assist the investigation. Their evidence helped convict Ali Kololo, who spent more than a decade in prison before his conviction was overturned.

Kololo is suing the Met, claiming a senior officer, former Detective Superintendent Neil Hibberd, gave misleading evidence at his trial and acted unlawfully to secure his conviction.

In his first media interview, he told the BBC about his 15-year ordeal and his fight for compensation, which the Met is challenging in court.

We meet on Lamu, a small island off Kenya's northern coast, once a thriving Swahili port. People and goods are still carted through its narrow stone streets by donkey rather than car.

It was here, in 2013, that Kololo was sentenced to death.

Standing at the jetty, where police once brought him ashore in handcuffs, he relishes being free. But he is struggling to rebuild his life.

"Everything was taken from me. I'm starting from zero. I don't think I'll ever go back to who I was before," he says.

David and Judith Tebbutt were on a dream holiday to Kenya when they were attacked

Before his arrest, Kololo lived with his wife and their three young children. He had once worked as a groundskeeper at the resort where the Tebbutts were staying, but by 2011 he earned his living felling trees in a local forest and selling the wood.

"My life was very good," he says. "I was fending for myself, taking good care of my family."

Within 24 hours of the attack, Kenyan police had arrested him.

"I was beaten with clubs and thrown into a car," he says. "They beat me for days, burning me with cigarettes, forcing me to confess to things. They subjected me to torture like no other."

Kololo could not read or write. He says police made him put his thumbprint on a statement claiming he had led the attackers to the Tebbutts.

"I didn't understand anything," he says, calling the statement "a mountain of lies". "I signed it without knowing what it was because of the state they had put me in".

The Kenyan police told us it "at all times strives to work within the law". Kololo is not suing them.

Ali Kololo says he lost contact with his children while he was in prison

Within days of the attack, a team of Met officers, led by then Detective Superintendent Neil Hibberd, arrived to support the Kenyan investigation. The UK government had instructed the officers not to accept information from the Kenyan authorities that had been obtained by interrogating detainees.

But Hibberd requested Kololo's statement and later relied on it when giving evidence for the prosecution at his trial.

In court, Hibberd also presented evidence linking Kololo to the attack. He told the Kenyan court Kololo had been wearing a type of shoe that matched footwear marks found in the sand at the resort.

The officer who had arrested Kololo said he was barefoot when he was handed to police. Hibberd did not disclose that the Met's own forensic examination could not establish whether the shoe in question had made the marks.

At the trial, Kololo did not initially have a lawyer. He had to cross-examine all the prosecution witnesses himself, including Hibberd, through an interpreter who spoke Swahili, which was not Kololo's first language.

"I believe I was framed because I am a poor man and I did not have the strength or means to fight for myself," Kololo says.

Kololo was convicted of kidnap and robbery with violence - the only person ever convicted in connection with the attack. He spent three years on death row before his sentence was commuted to life imprisonment.

He recalls seeing his prison file. In the space for the expiry date, someone had written "death".

"I was completely heartbroken. I believed I could be executed at any moment, and I would never see my family, my children, ever again."

Years later, the UK's Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) established that Hibberd had omitted significant forensic evidence at the trial. It found that he would have had a case to answer for gross misconduct, but he could not face disciplinary proceedings because he had retired from the force. At the time, his lawyer said Hibberd absolutely disagreed with the report's findings.

Neil Hibberd retired from the police in 2017

In April 2023, Kenya's High Court quashed Kololo's conviction, because of doubts over the prosecution's evidence. This followed years of work by the legal charity Reprieve and a Kenyan lawyer, Alfred Olaba, who represented him for free.

They were supported by Judith Tebbutt, who believed Kololo was innocent. In an interview with the BBC in 2022, she said he had been scapegoated by Scotland Yard.

"He was not there on the night. He was not part of the group that held me. They've put this man in prison without any real evidence."

More than three years after his release, Kololo says he is still living with the effects of his torture and decade in prison. As we walk the narrow streets of Lamu's old town, his thin frame moves stiffly. He is on edge. "My mind is not good," he says. "I have not recovered."

He remembers being kept in a filthy, bedbug-ridden cell with up to eight other inmates, which he thought he would never leave. Twice he contracted tuberculosis and nearly died.

Kololo is now too frail to do the woodcutting he once relied on to make a living. He tries to grow enough to eat on the land around his home, but erratic rain makes it difficult.

"I have nothing. On the days I get food, I eat, and on the days I don't, I endure."

He lives alone in a mud hut. His wife divorced him after he went to prison, and their children went to live with his mother. They dropped out of school because the family could not pay the fees. Kololo says they were not allowed to visit him in prison. When he was released, they barely remembered him, especially his youngest.

"They were too young. Only now are they starting to regain the memory that 'this is our father who disappeared'," he says. "If it weren't for my mother, my children might have died."

For much of our time together, Kololo is remarkably upbeat. He trusts that his lawyers and God will deliver him justice. But when we talk about the Met, his demeanour shifts.

"I am extremely angry with the police," he says. "I'm also angry with the Kenyan Police. They collaborated to incriminate me. What [Hibberd] said destroyed my entire life and my children's lives."

The Met has not apologised to Kololo or admitted wrongdoing. The force is contesting his compensation claim, which his lawyers say could take years to resolve.

"These people falsely accused me. Do I not deserve something?" he asks.

The Met told the BBC that neither they nor Hibberd wanted to comment on Kololo's claim, but it said: "Our thoughts are with Mr Kololo, Mrs Tebbutt, her family and all those who have been affected by this terrible crime. The Metropolitan Police remains committed to supporting the Kenyan authorities in any way that may be possible, in order to get justice for Mrs Tebbutt and her late husband."

Preetha Gopalan, Reprieve's head of UK litigation, describes the Met's behaviour in Kololo's case as "egregious".

"They've spent 10 years trying to evade accountability in every way possible, now dragging him through the courts," she says. "It's possible for them to do the right thing, but they are unwilling, and so this ordeal continues to haunt Kololo and his family."

"Even if I get a billion shillings, I will never be the same," Kololo says. "But if I get the justice I deserve, I can help my children and take care of myself when I am an old man."

If the ruling bloc cannot reach a deal, the country may have to go back to the polls

New Zealand's ruling coalition has fallen short of a parliamentary majority by one seat, following a campaign shaped by a sluggish economy and disillusioned voters.

It now needs the support of the centrist Opportunity Party to remain in power. If they cannot reach a deal, the country may have to go back to the polls.

The incumbent National Party led by Prime Minister Christopher Luxon secured 40 out of 130 seats, while its coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First took 13 and 12 respectively.

A government led by the centre-left Labour Party is not possible, official results on Friday show, as the bloc would not have enough seats even if Opportunity threw its weight behind it.

Labour secured 36 seats, The Greens took 17, while Te Pāti Māori, which represents Māori interests, picked up five.

Opportunity, which has been described as this election's kingmaker, secured seven seats. The party's leader Qiulae Wong has previously said she will negotiate first with the party that secures the largest number of seats.

Preliminary results on 7 November, election day, had projected that National combined with its coalition partners would have a slim lead over the left-leaning bloc.

But today's official tally shows it had lost two seats on special votes - cast by citizens who were overseas or outside of their registered electorate on election day - which typically skew left.

Some of National's key election pledges include lower taxes, cheaper energy, more renewable generation, and a greater focus on defence.

Labour, meanwhile, had campaigned to cut healthcare, public transport and fuel costs, more government support for social housing, among other things.

New Zealand's mixed-member proportional voting system means most governments are coalitions. Each voter makes two choices – for the representative of their constituency in parliament and a political party.

In earlier interviews with the BBC, many voters had expressed frustration over spiralling costs of living and high unemployment across the country, with declining faith in their political leadership.

"There's this kind of apathy and a bit of dread," said 21-year-old Imogen Vlutger.

A 40-year-old man said he didn't vote as he could not bring himself to tick any of the boxes on the ballot paper.

More than half of the country no longer see New Zealand as a land of opportunity, according to a survey by the Helen Clark Foundation, a public policy think tank.

Kiwis have been leaving the country in record numbers, with many of them, including former prime minister Jacinda Arden , moving to Australia.

MN202611_156j1pgbmte.t: Mu kiganiro kuri terefone yagiranye n’ingabo za Amerika ziri mu Buseruko bwo Hagati nijoro ku wa kane, mu birori vy’umusi mukuru w’amashimwe (uzwi nka Thanksgiving), Donald Trump yagarutse kenshi ku ntambara ya Irani, avuga ko “Amerika yinjiye muri iyo ntambara kandi iri muri ako karere atari kubera igitoro, ahubwo ari mu ntumbero yo gukingira Israel n’ibindi bihugu vyo muri ako karere.” Mu butumwa yahaye imirwi itandukanye y’ingabo za Amerika ikorera mu Buseruko bwo Hagati ari i Mar-a-Lago muri Florida, Perezida Trump yagize ati: “Ntidukeneye igitoro. Dufise ububiko bunini cane bw’igitoro, kandi hari na Venezuela, aho turonka amamiriyoni y’amatoni y’igitoro... “Ntitukeneye rero igitoro co mu Buseruko bwo Hagati, ariko dukeneye amahoro muri ako karere, kuko bitagenze gutyo hazoba ingorane nyinshi.” Trump yavuze kandi ko, uko abibona, iyo Reta Zunze Ubumwe za Amerika zitinjira muri iyo ntambara, Irani “yari gukoresha ibirwanisho ruhonyanganda vy’ubumara [vya nikleyeri] igatera Israel n’akarere kose, kandi isi iba yarahuye n’amahano atagira izina atewe n’ibirwanisho vya nikleyeri.” Irani ntihengeshanya guhakana ivyo yagirizwa ko yoba iriko igerageza guhingura ikibombe ca nikleyeri, kandi ko umugambi wayo wa nikleyeri atari uwa gisirikare. Irani kandi yagiriza Amerika ko yinjiye mu ntambara iri kumwe na Israel ku mohe n’imigambi ya Israel, atari kubera ico yita “ikibazo c’umutekano wa Reta Zunze Ubumwe za Amerika.” Ni mu gihe ubushikiranganji bwa Amerika bujejwe kwivuna abansi buvuga ko iyi ntambara yatanguye mu mpera za Ruhuhuma (2) uno mwaka imaze gutwara igisirikare ca Amerika hafi imiriyaridi 50 z’amadorari ya Amerika. Arthur Miller, ajejwe gutunganya no kugenzura amafaranga akoreshwa mu vya gisirikare, yavuze ko ayo mahera arimwo ayakoreshwa mu kugura amasasu n’ibirwanisho, ayo gusubiriza ibikoresho vya gisirikare vyononekaye canke vyakoreshejwe, hamwe n’amahera yakoreshejwe mu bikorwa vya gisirikare. Yasiguye ko muri ibi bitwara amafaranga menshi hatarimwo ivyononekaye mu bitero ku birindiro vya gisirikare vya Amerika biri mu Kigobe c’Abarabu, aho bimwe muri vyo vyasinzikaye cane mu bitero vy’amadrone (indege zitajamwo abadereva ) ya Irani, hamwe n’ibisasu vya misire vyarashwe na Irani muri iyi ntambara imaze amezi arenga icenda. Ayandi makuru ushobora gusoma: Amerika yemereye imiriyoni $20 umuntu wese azoyiha amakuru ku mugambi wa nikleyere wa Iran Ingaruka zishobora guterwa n'igabanuka ry'ibirwanisho ku ntambara yo muri Irani Ni ibihe bihugu bishyigikiye Iran mu ntambara irwana na Israel ifatanyije na Amerika?

A semi-truck carrying mail was left straddling an off-ramp and an overpass in Toledo, Ohio on Thanksgiving Day during severe weather in the US.

No injuries were reported, and authorities were able to pull the truck back onto the road, according to the BBC's US partner, CBS News.

The Ohio Department of Transportation described it as a "very unusual sight" before thanking emergency crews for helping "even on the holidays, even when it's cold and rainy".

MN202611_15pnv8zp1w1.t:
Refugee camp in Europe – This is the Idomeni informal refugee settlement at the Greco-Macedonian border, pictured here at its peak shortly after the closure of the Balkan route in March 2016. The camp was evacuated at the end of May. (Photo by Julian Buijzen/Flickr)

The hypocrisy surrounding Europe’s migration debate has become increasingly difficult to ignore. For years, migrants and asylum seekers have faced degrading treatment, exclusion, dangerous journeys and inhumane living conditions across parts of Europe.

Yet, the moment Rwanda offers to help provide a humanitarian solution, some European politicians and human rights organisations suddenly rediscover their concern for human dignity.

On November 16, 2026, five European Union member states namely Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands announced plans to work with Rwanda to establish an offshore return hub for rejected asylum seekers.

Rather than examining the proposal on its merits and considering how it could contribute to addressing a complex migration challenge, more than 70 European lawmakers have begun mobilising against it.

The lawmakers raise baseless accusations about Rwanda’s human rights record and dragging the conflict in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo into a debate that should primarily concern the welfare and future of migrants.

One cannot help but question this sudden enthusiasm for humanitarian principles. Where was this outrage when European countries struggled to provide humane treatment and dignified living conditions for migrants?

Where was the same energy when asylum seekers were subjected to hostility, discrimination, prolonged uncertainty, and dangerous conditions while attempting to reach European shores?

Where is the same concern for human rights when Europe pays some countries to stop migrants from crossing by all means, including detaining them indefinitely in inhumane conditions?

None of these so-called lawmakers and the army of self-styled human rights advocates can provide an answer to these questions.

Behind the theatrics deployed whenever Rwanda is invoked lies the assumption that dignity, safety, and humanitarian protection are privileges that only wealthy Western countries can provide. And perhaps Rwanda’s real fault is to tell a different story.

Since 2019, Rwanda has welcomed more than 3,200 African migrants evacuated from detention centres in Libya through emergency transit arrangements facilitated with international partners. Approximately 80% have subsequently been resettled in Europe and North America, while others have chosen to remain and rebuild their lives in Rwanda.

When the Taliban returned to power in Afghanistan in 2021, Rwanda welcomed students from the School of Leadership Afghanistan (SOLA), providing young Afghan girls with an opportunity to continue their education in safety.

Rwanda also facilitated the relocation of Sudanese medical students when conflict intensified in their country, allowing them to pursue their studies rather than abandon their academic ambitions.

These are practical examples of a country willing to extend solidarity to vulnerable people, regardless of their nationality or background.

The proposed arrangement with European countries follows a similar humanitarian philosophy. Rejected asylum seekers would be temporarily accommodated in facilities prepared for that purpose.

Rwanda would facilitate residence permits and support individuals in pursuing voluntary return to their countries of origin or resettlement in third countries. Those who choose to remain in Rwanda would have opportunities for integration into society through dedicated economic and social programmes.

Everyone must keep in mind that Rwanda did not create Europe’s migration crisis. It is not even pretending to resolve that problem. It is just offering a more humane model of dealing with it.

The real challenge originates primarily from the circumstances driving people out of their countries and the difficulties destination countries face in managing migration.

Rwanda’s humanitarian contribution to eradicating human trafficking and reducing the dangers associated with irregular migration should be told for what it is.

European lawmakers and human rights organisations are entitled to scrutinise the arrangement. But scrutiny must be consistent, evidence-based and free from prejudice.

Human rights should never become a convenient political instrument, invoked selectively when an African country takes an initiative that challenges established Western assumptions.

Instead of dismissing Rwanda’s contribution, perhaps these critics should examine the country’s experience and learn from its willingness to offer vulnerable people another chance.

The real measure of humanity is not the number of statements politicians make about human rights. It is what they do when vulnerable people need protection. Rwanda is offering to do something practical. Condemning that initiative without fairly examining its humanitarian potential is hypocrisy at its highest.

Adam Mweusi is a regional political analyst with expertise in security and geopolitical issue. He has written widely on Africa’s Renaissance.

MN202611_1dm63lhz02b.t:
Fines will rise steeply for both littering and more serious fly-tipping offences

People caught littering or illegally dumping waste in a north-west London borough are set to face higher fines as the council steps up its efforts to tackle persistent fly-tipping.

Harrow Council has approved plans to increase penalties for littering, breaches of Public Space Protection Orders (PSPOs) and the most serious fly-tipping offences.

Penalties for littering will rise from £500 to £750, with a reduced penalty of £300 available for early payment - the highest to be introduced in the capital under a new national maximum cap.

The penalty for breaching a PSPO will increase from £100 to £500, while a new £5,000 penalty will be introduced for the most serious fly-tipping offences.

The changes follow an increase in the maximum penalties available to councils under government rules.

The highest fly-tipping penalty will only be used in cases involving "aggravating factors", such as hazardous waste or repeat offences.

Other factors include the dumping of multiple bags, whether the waste affects vulnerable people, and whether it was dumped by a business for financial gain.

Speaking at a cabinet meeting where the proposal was approved last week, councillor Pritesh Patel said: "The reason for these changes is that the government has increased the maximum penalties available to councils. This gives us an opportunity to strengthen our response to environmental crime.

"Most people do the right thing, but there is a minority that don't, and it is important that the consequences are meaningful and encourage prompt compliance and resolutions."

Harrow Council has previously been criticised for its handling of fly-tipping

Harrow Council has tried a number of approaches to tackle fly-tipping over the years, including installing CCTV cameras in hotspots, sharing images and videos of offenders on social media and taking people to court.

But in January 2026, the council was criticised for failing to prosecute enough offenders at a fly-tipping hotspot in Harrow Weald.

Residents said a site on Weighton Road had to be cleared every few days. Despite a CCTV camera being in operation, only seven people had been sanctioned in the previous year.

One resident told a cabinet meeting in February that seven fines could be issued in a week, "let alone 52".

At the time, the council described the situation as "disgusting" following the long-running problems.

Housing has been the biggest issue for voters ahead of Spain's general election on Sunday, with millions of people protesting across the country in recent weeks over a lack of affordable homes.

Final opinion polls suggest the conservative People's Party will receive the most votes and that the right-wing Vox party is set to enter the national government for the first time. It would mean an end to Socialist prime minister Pedro Sánchez's eight years in power.

Europe correspondent Nick Beake speaks to a young couple from Valencia, who have been kept apart due to high rents in their city.

MN202611_1a2cn2b5jj5.t:
Reform UK is promising to scrap parking fees at NHS hospitals in England for all patients, visitors, and staff if it wins power at the next election.

The party said rising parking charges in recent years were unfair, with some hospitals charging up to £20 a day for parking spots.

It says it would compensate hospital trusts for the £300m they currently get from fees each year by raising more from foreign visitors using the NHS.

The health department said it expected charges to be reasonable, with fees used to maintain facilities or put towards funding health services.

Reform's announcement is part of a broader effort by the party to win credibility on the NHS, as it prepares to appoint someone who has worked in the NHS as its health spokesperson in the coming weeks.

Leader Nigel Farage's previous support for an insurance-based healthcare model has harmed the party's standing on the health service, insiders admit.

The latest policy is also part of a series designed to improve the party's recent struggles in the polls by addressing what Reform see as their perceived weaknesses, on Russia, on defence and now the NHS.

Reform's Treasury spokesman Robert Jenrick told the BBC the party's spending plans would be set closer to an election, but the party would ensure there would always be "real-terms increases" in funding for the NHS.

Echoing a line traditionally used by British politicians to claim stewardship of the health service, he said: "What we are saying is that the NHS is safe in our hands".

Parking at hospitals in Wales and Scotland is largely free, but NHS trusts in England are allowed to charge and set their own fees and rules.

Government guidance means parking is free for disabled people holding Blue Badges, frequent outpatients, parents of sick children staying overnight and NHS staff working night shifts.

But most visitors are generally expected to pay, along with staff working day shifts.

Reform says its policy to compensate NHS trusts would cost £285m a year to deliver, assuming a £25m annual saving from payment collection costs that would not longer be required.

It plans to recoup lost revenue by charging overseas visitors 200% of the national tariff for NHS services, instead of 150% currently, and extending charges to A&E visits, ambulance services and GP care.

It also says it would make all foreign visitors from countries that do not have reciprocal healthcare arrangements with the UK take out travel insurance covering NHS care, allowing it to "more aggressively collect" money due.

Siva Anandaciva, policy director at the King's Fund health think tank, said parking fees could be a "burden" for those visiting hospitals, but questioned whether Reform's proposals would raise enough to fully compensate trusts.

He said the additional charges on visitors for care would bring extra administration costs, whilst hospitals would need to spend money on systems to ensure free spaces were available to those who need them most.

The experience in Scotland had shown it can also take an "awfully long time" for hospitals to exit contracts with private firms running car pars, he said.

He added: "You might not end up saving as much money as you think".

The health department said it expected fees charged by trusts to be "reasonable and in line with the local area".

"Where charges do apply, the money made is used to maintain facilities, with surplus income put back into the NHS to benefit both staff and patients," a spokesperson added.

In response to parliamentary questions earlier this year, the department also argued , external fees were a "significant control mechanism" to manage capacity given the limited number of car parking spaces available.
